analysis.one_liner: Lets seniors trade Medicare Part A for a capped voucher for health savings accounts and high-deductible private plans.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted no cosponsors and died in committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let people entering Medicare give up their Part A hospital coverage and instead receive a voucher worth up to $200 a month, usable only to fund a health savings account or pay premiums on a high-deductible private insurance plan. It would also increase tax deductions for health savings account contributions by the voucher amount, and suspend Medicare late-enrollment penalties for people between 65 and 70. While enrolled in the voucher program, a person cannot use Medicare Part B or Part D, and a person who leaves the program to return to Medicare can never opt out again.
analysis.who_benefits: High-deductible health plan insurers and the financial firms that hold health savings accounts would gain a new, automatic funding stream from Medicare. A narrow group of healthy, financially savvy seniors who prefer private coverage would gain a tax-advantaged alternative, plus relief from late-enrollment penalties between 65 and 70.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurers and health savings account firms

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Medicare Alternative Voucher Program: a senior who waives Part A entitlement gets a monthly voucher capped at $200, usable only for health savings account contributions or high-deductible health plan premiums [S2][S3].

Amends the tax code so the amount of the voucher deposited into a health savings account increases that individual's allowable HSA tax deduction, removing the existing bar on HSA contributions once someone is Medicare-entitled [S2][S3].
Suspends Medicare Part B and Part D late-enrollment penalties for any month during which the person is between ages 65 and 70, which would help seniors who delay enrolling [S2][S3].

Establishes a procedure to waive Part A entitlement, addressing an administrative rule cited in the bill's findings that otherwise forced Social Security recipients into Part A whether or not they wanted it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Medicare trust fund and remaining traditional Medicare beneficiaries would bear the cost: healthier, wealthier seniors who opt out would remove their premiums from the traditional program's risk pool, leaving a sicker, more expensive pool of enrollees behind. Seniors in the voucher program would also be locked out of Part B and Part D while waived, and once they return to Medicare they can never waive again.
analysis.who_pays_short: Traditional Medicare and its remaining enrollees

drawbacks.text: The voucher is capped at $200 a month, which is likely far short of what a high-deductible plan costs a person in their late 60s, leaving a gap the senior must pay out of pocket [S3].

While enrolled in the voucher program, the person is ineligible for Medicare Part B (doctor visits) and Part D (drugs), so they would need separate private coverage for services the voucher does not pay for [S3].

The one-way door cuts both ways: a senior can end the waiver only during an annual window and, after returning to Medicare, can never opt out again — so a person who develops a serious illness and miscalculates has no second chance [S3].

If healthier seniors opt out of Part A, the traditional Medicare risk pool becomes sicker and more expensive for everyone who stays, a standard critique of Medicare voucher proposals that an honest supporter would have to address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine wins here are narrow: more choice for a small group of seniors who want private coverage, and relief from late-enrollment penalties for 65-to-70-year-olds. The costs are structural. Routing Medicare money through health savings accounts and high-deductible private plans shifts public health dollars toward insurers and financial firms, invites healthier seniors out of the shared insurance pool, and exposes seniors who misjudge their health to being priced out of private coverage with only one chance to come back. On balance, the bill's main effect would be entrenching a private alternative at public expense, with modest choice benefits for a few.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, no cosponsor ever signed on, and neither committee took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on November 19, 2015 [S1].
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
Both committees referred it to their health subcommittees on November 19 and 20, 2015, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill never attracted a single cosponsor [S4].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without the bill receiving a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Traditional Medicare and its beneficiaries, since a voucher program that would have pulled healthier seniors out of the shared insurance pool never advanced. High-deductible plan insurers and health savings account firms lost a potential new revenue stream.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Traditional Medicare enrollees, by the bill dying

sides.party_line_note: Only a Republican sponsored the bill and no member of either party cosponsored it, so no partisan divide ever formed; the bill simply drew no support.

industries.note: The bill would create a new class of customers by allowing seniors to use a Medicare voucher to pay premiums on high-deductible private plans. Insurers would gain revenue, though from plans that shift most costs onto the seniors themselves.
The bill routes voucher money into HSAs and raises the tax deduction for those contributions, expanding assets under management at HSA trustees and banks.
If healthier seniors waive Part A, the remaining pool of traditional Medicare enrollees becomes sicker and more expensive, raising costs for the program and the people who stay in it.
